interactions.summary: The host asks how long the Ukraine war can continue under Jiang's predictive-history model.
Jiang says Putin wants to prolong the war because battlefield dominance lets him lure NATO into an unwinnable Odessa commitment that destabilizes Europe from within.
The host pivots to Sino-American relations, asking about tariffs, the next three years under Trump, and whether China still needs the U.S. export market.

Jiang says the United States and China remain deeply codependent, that Trump is using pressure to force concessions before a likely rapprochement, and that America's soft power still shapes Chinese aspirations.

claims.claim: Jiang says Putin benefits from dragging out the Ukraine war because he is already winning on the battlefield and wants to force NATO into an unpopular ground commitment in Odessa.
He argues Putin's real objective is regime change in Britain, France, and Germany by maximizing conflict between European elites and their populations.
Jiang says China and the United States have been codependent for roughly thirty years and that Xi Jinping's rise strained that friendship.
He says Trump is applying economic pressure to weaken Xi domestically and extract economic concessions, not to fully sever the relationship.
Jiang predicts Trump will visit China by the end of the year and that this will begin a rapprochement between the two countries.
He argues there is no real replacement for China's manufacturing base despite years of talk about Vietnam, India, or Southeast Asia.
Jiang says Chinese families are still strongly drawn to America because of soft power, education, and the dream of moving money and family there.

signature_moments.moment: Putin is said to win not by conquering NATO directly but by dragging it into a war that tears its own societies apart.
signature_moments.source_phrase: dragging them into an unwinnable war
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It sharpens Jiang's reading of the Ukraine war as a regime-destabilization trap for Europe.

signature_moments.moment: The U.S.-China relationship is framed less as decoupling than as a damaged friendship that still cannot fully separate.
signature_moments.source_phrase: have been best friends basically for the past 30 years
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This gives the trade-war discussion a more intimate, codependent frame than standard great-power rivalry language.

signature_moments.moment: The Chinese dream is rendered as making enough money to move your family to America.
signature_moments.source_phrase: The Chinese dream is to make as much money as you can so that you can move your money and your family to America
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It is one of the interview's most provocative soft-power formulations and likely to matter in the public read.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Jiang's description of the long U.S.-China relationship: deeply intertwined, strained under Xi, but still not replaceable.
Jiang's expected end-state in which pressure tactics give way to renewed practical cooperation and concessions between Washington and Beijing.

chronology_notes.note: On 2025-07-23 Jiang makes a dated U.S.-China forecast for the remainder of the year: pressure now, Trump visit later, and the beginning of rapprochement by year-end.
